questions.problem:
Two fair  four-sided dice are rolled and $X$ is the absolute difference of their scores. The probability mass function $f(x)$ of $X$ is shown in the table below. What is $\text{Var}[X]?$ 

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $\frac{2}{8}$ | $\frac{3}{8}$ | $\frac{2}{8}$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ |
questions.worked_solution:
The variance of a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S$ is given by

$$
\text{Var}[X]={\sum }_{x\in S}(x-\text{E}[X])^{2}\cdot f(x).
$$

First, we need to compute $\text{E}[X].$ Summing up the products of each value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =0\cdot f(0)+1\cdot f(1)+2\cdot f(2)+3\cdot f(3) \\  & =0(\frac{2}{8})+1(\frac{3}{8})+2(\frac{2}{8})+3(\frac{1}{8}) \\  & =\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[X]=\frac{5}{4}$ into the variance formula, we get

$$
\text{Var}[X]={\sum }_{x\in S}{(x-\frac{5}{4})}^{2}\cdot f(x).
$$

Now, we compute the variance as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & ={(0-\frac{5}{4})}^{2}\cdot f(0)+{(1-\frac{5}{4})}^{2}\cdot f(1)+{(2-\frac{5}{4})}^{2}\cdot f(2)+{(3-\frac{5}{4})}^{2}\cdot f(3) \\  & ={(-\frac{5}{4})}^{2}\cdot f(0)+{(-\frac{1}{4})}^{2}\cdot f(1)+{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}\cdot f(2)+{(\frac{7}{4})}^{2}\cdot f(3) \\  & =(\frac{25}{16})(\frac{2}{8})+(\frac{1}{16})(\frac{3}{8})+(\frac{9}{16})(\frac{2}{8})+(\frac{49}{16})(\frac{1}{8}) \\  & =\frac{15}{16}\end{aligned}
$$

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $\frac{256}{625}$ | $\frac{256}{625}$ | $\frac{96}{625}$ | $\frac{16}{625}$ | $\frac{1}{625}$ |
questions.worked_solution:
We can compute the variance of a discrete random variable $X$ using the following formula:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}
$$

First, we compute $\text{E}[X].$ Summing up the products of each value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =0\cdot f(0)+1\cdot f(1)+2\cdot f(2)+3\cdot f(3)+4\cdot f(4) \\  & =0(\frac{256}{625})+1(\frac{256}{625})+2(\frac{96}{625})+3(\frac{16}{625})+4(\frac{1}{625}) \\  & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}].$ Summing up the products of each value of ${X}^{2}$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={0}^{2}\cdot f(1)+{1}^{2}\cdot f(2)+{2}^{2}\cdot f(3)+{3}^{2}\cdot f(4)+{4}^{2}\cdot f(5) \\  & =0(\frac{256}{625})+1(\frac{256}{625})+4(\frac{96}{625})+9(\frac{16}{625})+16(\frac{1}{625}) \\  & =\frac{32}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{32}{25}-{(\frac{4}{5})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{32}{25}-\frac{16}{25} \\  & =\frac{16}{25}.\end{aligned}

questions.worked_solution:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}
$$

$$

Next, we compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}].$ Summing up the products of each value of ${X}^{2}$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={1}^{2}\cdot f(1)+{2}^{2}\cdot f(2)+{3}^{2}\cdot f(3)+{4}^{2}\cdot f(4)+{5}^{2}\cdot f(5)+{6}^{2}\cdot f(6) \\  & =1(\frac{1}{8})+4(\frac{3}{8})+9(\frac{1}{4})+16(\frac{1}{8})+25(\frac{1}{16})+36(\frac{1}{16}) \\  & =\frac{155}{16}.\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
Two fair  four-sided dice are rolled and $X$ is the absolute difference of their scores. The probability mass function $f(x)$ of $X$ is shown in the table below. What is $\text{SD}[X]?$ 

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{3}{8}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ |
questions.worked_solution:
The standard deviation of a random variable $X$ is defined as

$$
\text{SD}[X]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[X]},
$$

where the variance can be computed using the following formula:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}
$$

First, we need to compute $\text{E}[X].$ Summing up the products of each value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =0\cdot f(0)+1\cdot f(1)+2\cdot f(2)+3\cdot f(3) \\  & =0(\frac{1}{4})+1(\frac{3}{8})+2(\frac{1}{4})+3(\frac{1}{8}) \\  & =\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}].$ Summing up the products of each value of ${X}^{2}$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={0}^{2}\cdot f(0)+{1}^{2}\cdot f(1)+{2}^{2}\cdot f(2)+{3}^{2}\cdot f(3) \\  & =0(\frac{1}{4})+1(\frac{3}{8})+4(\frac{1}{4})+9(\frac{1}{8}) \\  & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the variance is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}-{(\frac{5}{4})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}-\frac{25}{16} \\  & =\frac{15}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{SD}[X] & =\sqrt{\text{Var}[X]} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{15}{16}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{15}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $X$ be the number obtained by a fair spinner with five sections labeled $-2,-1,1,2,3.$ What is $\text{SD}[X]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The standard deviation of a random variable $X$ is defined as

$$
\text{SD}[X]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[X]},
$$

where the variance can be computed using the following formula:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}
$$

First, we need to compute the probability mass function $f(x).$ Here, there are $5$ possible outcomes ($-2,-1,1,2,3$) and each outcome has the same probability, so the probability mass function is as follows:

| $x$ | $-2$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $\frac{1}{5}$ | $\frac{1}{5}$ | $\frac{1}{5}$ | $\frac{1}{5}$ | $\frac{1}{5}$ |

Next, we compute $\text{E}[X].$ Summing up the products of each value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =(-2)\cdot f(-2)+(-1)\cdot f(-1)+1\cdot f(1)+2\cdot f(2)+3\cdot f(3) \\  & =(-2)(\frac{1}{5})+(-1)(\frac{1}{5})+1(\frac{1}{5})+2(\frac{1}{5})+3(\frac{1}{5}) \\  & =\frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}].$ Summing up the products of each value of ${X}^{2}$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & =(-2)^{2}\cdot f(-2)+(-1)^{2}\cdot f(-1)+{1}^{2}\cdot f(1)+{2}^{2}\cdot f(2)+{3}^{2}\cdot f(3) \\  & =4(\frac{1}{5})+1(\frac{1}{5})+1(\frac{1}{5})+4(\frac{1}{5})+9(\frac{1}{5}) \\  & =\frac{19}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the variance is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{19}{5}-{(\frac{3}{5})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{19}{5}-\frac{9}{25} \\  & =\frac{95}{25}-\frac{9}{25} \\  & =\frac{86}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{SD}[X] & =\sqrt{\text{Var}[X]} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{86}{25}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{86}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Let $X$ be the number obtained by a spinner with four sections labeled $1, 2, 3, 4.$ The probability mass function $f(x)$ of $X$ is shown in the table below. What is $\textrm{Var}[X]?$

| $x$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $\dfrac{1}{6}$ | $\dfrac{1}{4}$ | $\dfrac{1}{3}$ | $\dfrac{1}{4}$ |
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The variance of a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S$ is given by

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \sum\limits_{x \in S} (x - \textrm E[X])^2 \cdot f(x).
$$

First, we need to compute $\textrm E[X].$ Summing up the products of each value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =1\cdot f(1)+2\cdot f(2)+3\cdot f(3)+4\cdot f(4) \\  & =1(\frac{1}{6})+2(\frac{1}{4})+3(\frac{1}{3})+4(\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\textrm E[X]=\dfrac{8}{3}$ into the variance formula, we get

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \sum\limits_{x \in S} \left(x - \dfrac{8}{3} \right)^2 \cdot f(x).
$$

Now, we compute the variance as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & ={(1-\frac{8}{3})}^{2}\cdot f(1)+{(2-\frac{8}{3})}^{2}\cdot f(2)+{(3-\frac{8}{3})}^{2}\cdot f(3)+{(4-\frac{8}{3})}^{2}\cdot f(4) \\  & =\frac{25}{9}\cdot f(1)+\frac{4}{9}\cdot f(2)+\frac{1}{9}\cdot f(3)+\frac{16}{9}\cdot f(4) \\  & =\frac{25}{9}(\frac{1}{6})+\frac{4}{9}\cdot (\frac{1}{4})+\frac{1}{9}\cdot (\frac{1}{3})+\frac{16}{9}(\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{19}{18}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We can compute the variance of a discrete random variable $X$ using the following formula:

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \textrm E[X^2] - \textrm E[X]^2
$$

First, we need to compute the probability mass function $f(x).$ Here, there are $6$ possible outcomes ($1,2,3,4,5,6$) and each outcome has the same probability, so the probability mass function is as follows:

| $x$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ | $5$ | $6$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $\dfrac{1}{6}$ | $\dfrac{1}{6}$ | $\dfrac{1}{6}$ | $\dfrac{1}{6}$ | $\dfrac{1}{6}$ | $\dfrac{1}{6}$ |

Next, we compute $\textrm E[X].$ Summing up the products of each value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =1\cdot f(1)+2\cdot f(2)+3\cdot f(3)+4\cdot f(4)+5\cdot f(5)+6\cdot f(6) \\  & =1(\frac{1}{6})+2(\frac{1}{6})+3(\frac{1}{6})+4(\frac{1}{6})+5(\frac{1}{6})+6(\frac{1}{6}) \\  & =\frac{7}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute $\textrm E[X^2].$ Summing up the products of each value of $X^2$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={1}^{2}\cdot f(1)+{2}^{2}\cdot f(2)+{3}^{2}\cdot f(3)+{4}^{2}\cdot f(4)+{5}^{2}\cdot f(5)+{6}^{2}\cdot f(6) \\  & =1(\frac{1}{6})+4(\frac{1}{6})+9(\frac{1}{6})+16(\frac{1}{6})+25(\frac{1}{6})+36(\frac{1}{6}) \\  & =\frac{91}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{91}{6}-{(\frac{7}{2})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{91}{6}-\frac{49}{4} \\  & =\frac{35}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={1}^{2}\cdot f(1)+{2}^{2}\cdot f(2)+{3}^{2}\cdot f(3)+{4}^{2}\cdot f(4)+{5}^{2}\cdot f(5)+{6}^{2}\cdot f(6) \\  & =1(\frac{1}{6})+4(\frac{1}{6})+9(\frac{1}{6})+16(\frac{1}{6})+25(\frac{1}{6})+36(\frac{1}{6}) \\  & =\frac{91}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{91}{6}-{(\frac{7}{2})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{91}{6}-\frac{49}{4} \\  & =\frac{35}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{SD}[X] & =\sqrt{\text{Var}[X]} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{35}{12}}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The **variance** of a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S$ is given by

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \sum\limits_{x \in S} (x - \textrm E[X])^2 \cdot f(x).
$$

In other words, the variance is the expected value of the squared difference between $X$ and the expected value of $X{:}$

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \textrm E [ (X - \textrm E[X])^2 ]
$$

The variance quantifies how "spread out" a probability distribution is. The expected value $\textrm E[X]$ can be interpreted as the "center" of a probability distribution, and the squared difference $(X - \textrm E[X])^2$ represents the squared distance between $X$ and the center. So, the variance quantifies how far the possible values of $X$ are from the center, on average.

In general,

- a probability distribution that is *spread out* over many possible values will have a *high* variance, while

- a probability distribution that is *concentrated* (or *clumped*) near a single value will have a *low* variance.

tutorials.name: Proving the Formula For the Variance in Terms of First and Second Raw Moments
tutorials.problem:
We wish to prove the following formula for the variance:

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \textrm{E}[X^2] - \textrm{E}[X]^2
$$

To begin, recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is defined as

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \textrm E [ (X - \textrm E[X])^2 ].
$$

Expanding out the perfect square, we get

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] =\textrm E [ X^2 - 2\textrm E[X] \cdot X + \textrm E[X]^2 ] .
$$

Then, distributing the expectation over the sum, we get

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \textrm E [ X^2 ] + \textrm E[ - 2\textrm E[X] \cdot X ] + \textrm E[ \textrm E[X]^2 ] .
$$

Now, we make the following simplifications:

- Since $\textrm E[aX] = a \textrm E[X]$ for any constant $a,$ we can write

$$
\textrm E[{\color{blue}-2 \textrm E[X]} \cdot X] = {\color{blue}- 2\textrm E[X]} \cdot \textrm E[ X ] = - 2\textrm E[X]^2.
$$

- Since $\textrm{E}[X]$ is a constant, and $\textrm E[a] = a$ for any constant $a,$ we can write

$$
\textrm E[ {\color{blue}\textrm E[X]^2} ] = {\color{blue}\textrm E[X]^2}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]+\text{E}[-2\text{E}[X]\cdot X]+\text{E}[E[X]^{2}] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-2\text{E}[X]^{2}+\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
